blocks.prompt: How an Orange Is Built
blocks.text: An orange grows on a tree with dark green leaves. The tree flowers first. The flowers are white and they smell sweet. Then each flower turns into a small green ball, and the ball grows all summer. When you peel an orange, you find it is already built in pieces. Each piece is a segment. Inside each segment are hundreds of tiny juice sacs, packed tight like little water balloons. When you bite down, the sacs pop. That is why your chin gets wet.

blocks.prompt: The Fruit That Named the Color
blocks.text: Here is a strange thing about the orange. The fruit came first. The color was named after it. Long ago, English speakers did not have a word for the color orange. If they wanted to describe a carrot or a bright sunset, they had to call it yellow-red. That was the only word they had. Then traders began carrying a round, sweet fruit north from Asia. Sellers shouted its name in the markets. The name traveled from language to language for hundreds of years, changing a little each time, until English speakers were calling it an orange. The fruit was everywhere. People pointed at it. And slowly, when they wanted to describe a carrot or a sunset, they stopped saying yellow-red and started saying orange, like the fruit. So the color did not name the fruit. The fruit named the color. Every orange traffic cone and orange pumpkin and orange sunset carries the name of a piece of fruit from a tree in Asia.

blocks.prompt: One Tree, Everywhere
blocks.text: Pick up a navel orange and look at the bottom. There is a small pucker there that looks like a belly button. That is where the name comes from. But the pucker is not a belly button. It is a second orange, tiny and unfinished, growing inside the first one. That happened by accident. Around two hundred years ago, at a monastery in Bahia, Brazil, one branch on one orange tree started producing strange fruit. The oranges had the little twin inside. They were also sweeter than the rest, easy to peel, and completely seedless. Seedless is wonderful for eating and terrible for farming. A seedless orange cannot make a new tree. So growers took the only other route. They cut small pieces off that branch and grafted them onto other citrus roots. Each graft grew into a tree that made the same fruit. Then they cut pieces off those trees and grafted again. In 1873 a few of those grafted trees arrived in Riverside, California. They thrived, and California cut more pieces off them. Today every navel orange in every store on Earth traces back, cutting by cutting, to that one lucky branch in Brazil. They are not relatives. They are copies. Biologists call an orchard like that a clone, and the whole navel orange business is one enormous tree, spread thin across the world.

blocks.prompt: The Fruit That Won at Sea
blocks.text: For hundreds of years, long ocean voyages killed sailors, and nobody knew why. The disease was called scurvy, and it was grotesque. Gums swelled and bled. Old wounds that had healed years earlier split open again. Teeth loosened. Skin bruised at a touch. On some voyages scurvy killed more men than storms, shipwreck, and battle combined. The cause is almost embarrassing in its simplicity. Human bodies cannot make vitamin C. Almost every other mammal can, but somewhere in our ancestry the gene that builds it broke, and it stayed broken. Without vitamin C, the body cannot properly build collagen, the protein that holds skin, blood vessels, and old scars together. Deny a person vitamin C for a few months and the body slowly comes apart at the seams. That is all scurvy is. In 1747 a Scottish naval doctor named James Lind ran what many people call the first controlled clinical trial. He took twelve sick sailors, divided them into six pairs, and gave each pair a different supposed cure: cider, seawater, vinegar, a sulfuric acid mixture, a paste of herbs, and, to the last pair, two oranges and a lemon a day. The citrus pair recovered so fast that one of them was fit for duty within a week. Lind published his results. The navy took nearly fifty more years to act on them. When it finally did, and issued citrus to its crews, scurvy nearly vanished from the fleet. There is a lesson in the delay. Lind had the evidence, but he did not know why citrus worked, and he buried the finding in a long book among his other theories. Vitamin C itself was not identified until the 1930s. Good evidence, badly explained and quietly published, can sit unused for decades while people keep dying of a solved problem.

6.title: The Fruit That Named a Color
6.subtitle: A reading and analysis sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Fruit That Named a Color

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Citrus sinensis: a pomelo and mandarin hybrid
No sweet orange grows wild anywhere
The name lost its first letter in Europe
Navel oranges are grafts of one 1820s branch
Citrus greening cut Florida output over ninety percent
Greek, Romanian, and Arabic name it after Portugal

blocks.prompt: Every Navel Orange Is the Same Tree
blocks.text: The orange is not a wild fruit. There is no forest anywhere on Earth where sweet oranges grow on their own. The sweet orange, Citrus sinensis, is a hybrid, a cross between the pomelo and the mandarin, and it was made by people in southern Asia thousands of years ago. Every orange you have ever eaten is a human invention that happens to be alive. You can hear that history in the word itself. The name began in India as naranga, moved into Persian as narang, into Arabic as naranj, and along the trade routes into Italian and French, losing its first letter somewhere on the way, probably because 'a naranj' kept getting misheard as 'an aranj.' English received it around the fourteenth century. The color came later. Before the fruit arrived, English had no word for that shade at all. A carrot or a sunset was simply yellow-red. The fruit named the color, and not the other way around, which is why every traffic cone and pumpkin on Earth is quietly named after a piece of fruit from Asia. In Greek and Romanian and Arabic, meanwhile, the word for the fruit comes from Portugal, because Portuguese ships were the ones that carried the sweet ones west. Then there is the navel orange, which is a stranger story. Look at the base of one and you will find a small pucker. That is a second orange, tiny and unfinished, growing inside the first. It is a mutation, and it began on a single branch of a single tree at a monastery in Bahia, Brazil, around two hundred years ago. The fruit from that branch was sweeter, easier to peel, and seedless. Seedless is the whole problem. A seedless orange cannot start a new tree, so the only way to keep the mutation is to cut a piece off the branch and graft it onto other citrus rootstock. In 1873 three grafted cuttings reached Eliza Tibbets in Riverside, California. Two survived, and California cut pieces off those, and pieces off those. Today every navel orange in every store in the world is a graft of a graft of a graft, tracing back to that one branch. They are not a variety. They are a single organism, cut into millions of pieces and stuck in the ground. That is efficient, and it is dangerous. A clone has no genetic variation, which means it has no argument to make against a disease that happens to defeat it. Citrus greening, caused by a bacterium carried by a small insect called the Asian citrus psyllid, reached Florida in 2005. The bacterium starves the tree, the fruit stays green and bitter and drops early, and the tree dies. There is no cure. Florida's orange production has fallen by more than ninety percent since the disease took hold. A grove of a million genetically identical trees is not a million defenses against that. It is one defense, tried a million times, failing a million times. So the orange is worth more than a lunchbox slot. It is a record of trade routes, a mutation kept alive by knife and patience for two centuries, and a live demonstration of what happens when you decide, at scale, that you never want a surprise again.
